title: Colonial rule
hookLine: from the 1700s to the 1900s, much of the Muslim world came under European rule

lines: A CLASSROOM MAP, SHADED IN COLORS.
LAY THE MUSLIM WORLD OVER IT.
cards: A school map, the kind that once hung on classroom walls, shaded in a few colors, one for each European empire. Now lay a second map over it: where Muslims lived.
From North Africa to the Indian Ocean, from West Africa to the islands of Southeast Asia, much of it sits under the colors of the first.

Behind every patch are real towns, mosques and families, ruled within a lifetime by people from far away. That's a lot for one lesson, so this one is about one thing: how to tell it. Today: colonial rule.

teach.h: EUROPEAN EMPIRES ACROSS THE MUSLIM WORLD.
teach.b: Over the modern centuries, European powers came to rule a great deal of the Muslim world. The British in India and Egypt. The French in Algeria.
The Dutch in the islands we now call Indonesia. The stories differ from place to place, and an honest telling keeps them different. Some of what came was conquest, war and land taken.
Some was railways, telegraph lines and schools, built mostly to serve the rulers and later put to use by the ruled. Borders were drawn by people who would never live inside them.
Old institutions, like the endowments we've been meeting, were in some places taken over or redirected.
Muslims answered in many ways, and they didn't agree with each other. Some took up arms. Some opened new schools.
Some worked inside the colonial system and tried to soften it. Some went into exile. One life refuses a simple telling.

Emir Abdelkader led years of armed resistance to the French in Algeria, lost, and was eventually exiled. Later, living in Damascus, he saw mobs turn on the city's Christians, and he and his men sheltered many of them.
A fighter against a European empire, protecting Christians from a Muslim mob. Both true. The Qur'an asks for this honesty.
In Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred." Justice even against your own side.
So name the harm plainly, name those who resisted and those who didn't, and leave nobody out because they spoil the story. Told honestly.

how: Muslim communities remember the colonial period in many ways, from national holidays and museums to the stories of grandparents, and Muslim historians and scholars continue to debate how it changed religious life.

games.q: you're Emir Abdelkader, exiled in Damascus after years fighting a European empire. a mob turns on the city's Christians. what do you do?
o: stay out of it. they're not your people.
shelter them in your own household.
leave the city until it's over.
games.why: he and his men sheltered many of the city's Christians. a fighter against an empire, and a protector of his Christian neighbors. both true.

practice: Bring to mind one Muslim-majority country, maybe your family's, maybe one you know only from the news. Hold three plain questions beside it: who ruled it, and from where; what did people lose; who resisted, and how?
If you pray, remember its people; if not, let the place stay in mind as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Colonial rule. The long stretch when European empires ruled much of the Muslim world, a history to be told with justice, even when it's uncomfortable. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the modern word for colonialism.

carryVoice: Your line: told honestly. The hard parts and the brave parts both belong. Rest easy until tomorrow.
